newsitem.title: USA: Consultant sues First Union, alleging fraud.
newsitem.headline: Consultant sues First Union, alleging fraud.

text.p: A consultant hired by a First Union Corp unit to provide brokerage and marketing services has sued the bank, alleging it fraudulently misled him and HSBC Holdings Plc's Marine Midland Bank with exaggerated financial statements.
A subpoena issued to Haim Branisteanu and obtained by Reuters last month indicated that the U.S. Attorney's office in Newark, N.J., is also looking for information regarding the matter.

According to the complaint, filed this week in New Jersey Superior Court by Branisteanu, First Fidelity Bank made "intentionally false" statements "which were intended to fraudulently induce Branisteanu to enter into an agreement to assist First Fidelity" in selling a non-performing loan.
First Union, which acquired First Fidelity last year, said through a spokesman that it is bank policy not to comment on pending litigation.
The allegations center on a $14 million loan First Fidelity made to Robert Ciasulli, owner of a New Jersey car dealership.
First Fidelity hired Branisteanu to find a bank to refinance the loan after Ciasulli defaulted, according to the complaint.

After Branisteanu interested Marine Midland in the refinancing, he allegedly discovered serious problems with the documents First Fidelity supplied to detail Ciasulli's financial picture, according to the complaint.

"First Fidelity was fully aware that Ciasulli routinely overstated his net worth by millions of dollars on his financial statements, regularly underreported his income to the taxing authorities, and faced significant exposure in a continuing divorce litigation with his former wife," the complaint alleges.
Branisteanu said he tried to alert top officials at First Fidelity about the problems with Ciasulli's financial information, but they told him not to get involved.
Ciasulli's attorney, Robert Woehling, said he had not yet seen Branisteanu's complaint and had no comment.
Branisteanu asked the court to force First Union to pay him at least $300,000 in compensatory damages and $300,000 in punitive damages, plus interest and attorneys fees.
